trial_name: REACT-2 — Immediate Total-Body CT Scanning vs Conventional Imaging & Selective CT in Severe Trauma (2016)
citation: Sierink JC, Treskes K, Edwards MJR, Beuker BJA, den Hartog D, Hohmann J, et al; REACT-2 study group. Immediate total-body CT scanning versus conventional imaging and selective CT scanning in patients with severe trauma (REACT-2): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2016;388(10045):673-683.
trial_type: RCT — multicentre, randomised, controlled, parallel-group, open-label
one_liner: In adults with suspected severe trauma, immediate total-body CT shortened diagnostic process times but did not reduce in-hospital mortality compared to conventional imaging and selective CT.

pico.population: Adult trauma patients (≥18 years) with suspected severe injury based on compromised vital parameters (SBP <100 mmHg, HR >120 bpm, GCS <14, RR >30 or <10 bpm), clinical suspicion of major thoracic/abdominal/pelvic/fracture injury, or high-risk mechanisms.
pico.intervention: Immediate total-body CT (iTBCT) from head to pelvis performed as a standardized two-step protocol during initial resuscitation after primary survey.
pico.comparison: Standard work-up comprising conventional radiography and FAST followed by selective CT based on clinical criteria and physician judgment.
pico.outcome: Primary: In-hospital mortality. Key secondary: 24-hour and 30-day mortality, diagnostic process times, radiation exposure, 6-month readmissions, and hospital costs.

background.existing_knowledge: Whole-body CT ('pan-scan') became common in high-resource trauma centers driven by diagnostic completeness and the premise that earlier injury mapping improves triage to surgery, IR, or ICU. Pre-REACT-2 evidence was predominantly observational registry data with high risk of confounding by indication.
background.knowledge_gap: Lack of high-quality randomized evidence evaluating whether routine immediate whole-body CT improves patient-centered endpoints (mortality) compared to selective CT, given potential harms including radiation, contrast exposure, resource strain, and workflow interruption.
background.hypothesis: Immediate total-body CT reduces in-hospital mortality by accelerating diagnosis and definitive management without unacceptable harms.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, controlled, parallel-group, open-label trial at 5 level-1 trauma centres (4 in Netherlands, 1 in Switzerland).
methods.setting: Emergency department trauma resuscitation room during initial evaluation immediately upon patient arrival.

inclusion: Suspected severe injury based on vital sign compromise (SBP <100 mmHg, HR >120 bpm, GCS <14, RR >30 or <10/min)
Clinical suspicion of major thoracic, abdominal, or pelvic injury, or multiple long-bone fractures
High-risk trauma mechanisms (fall >3 m, ejection from vehicle, run over/crush)
exclusion: Requirement for immediate CPR or immediate emergency operative intervention with imminent death (too unstable to randomize)

methods.intervention: Immediate total-body CT (iTBCT): standardized head-to-pelvis CT protocol (vertex to pubic symphysis; 64-slice scanners, IV contrast where appropriate) replacing standard sequence after initial primary survey.
methods.comparison: Standard work-up: conventional X-rays plus FAST sonography, followed by selective CT of specific regions based on pre-specified criteria and clinician judgment. Additional rescue imaging permitted in both arms.
methods.blinding: Open-label (unblinded to treating clinicians and patients; objective primary mortality endpoint).
methods.sample_size_power: 539 patients per group needed to detect a 5% absolute mortality reduction (12% to 7%) with 80% power at two-sided 5% significance level.
secondary_outcomes: Radiation exposure in trauma room and total hospital admission
Serious adverse events related to CT
methods.follow_up: Index admission for primary endpoint; pre-specified secondary follow-up at 30 days and 6 months.

headline_bullets: In-hospital mortality was identical between immediate total-body CT and standard selective work-up (16% vs 16%, P=0.92).
Immediate total-body CT significantly reduced diagnostic process times, including time to end of imaging (30 vs 37 min) and time to diagnosis (50 vs 58 min, both P<0.0001).
Radiation exposure was higher in the immediate total-body CT group during trauma room resuscitation (20.9 vs 20.6 mSv, P<0.0001).
Readmission within 6 months was unexpectedly higher in the iTBCT group (17% vs 11%, P=0.01), with no difference in overall 6-month costs.

outcomes_table.note: Excludes trauma-room deaths and protocol exclusions

outcomes_table.outcome: Time to end of imaging (min), median (IQR)

outcomes_table.note: More patients in standard group received lower doses
Distributional shift toward higher early radiation

outcomes_table.outcome: Serious adverse events related to CT scanning
outcomes_table.note: 5 serious events overall, all resulted in death (1 in post-randomisation excluded patient)

subgroup_table.subgroup: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) subgroup in-hospital mortality

safety: Serious adverse events related to CT scanning occurred in 3/541 (1%) in iTBCT vs 1/542 (<1%) in standard work-up.
Five serious adverse events were reported overall across the trial, all resulting in death (including 1 patient excluded post-randomisation).
Radiation exposure was significantly higher in the iTBCT group during trauma room evaluation (20.9 vs 20.6 mSv, P<0.0001) and total hospital stay (21.0 vs 20.6 mSv, P<0.0001).

domains.notes: 1:1 computerised randomisation (ALEA) following primary survey in the trauma resuscitation room across mature level-1 trauma centres.
Open-label trial design; primary endpoint (in-hospital mortality) is objective, but workflow and process timing endpoints are susceptible to unblinded clinical performance effects.
1403 patients randomised, but only 1083 (77% in each arm: 541 iTBCT, 542 selective CT) were included in primary analysis due to post-randomisation exclusions for consent or eligibility criteria.
Crossovers occurred (6 in iTBCT vs 18 in standard arm); protocol violation rate was ~9%. Post-hoc per-protocol sensitivity analysis excluding crossovers yielded identical conclusions.
Well-balanced for median age (42 vs 45 years), male sex (76% vs 76%), median ISS (20 vs 19), and hypotension (7% vs 8%). Slight imbalance in polytrauma (67% vs 61%) and TBI (33% vs 28%).

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate: causal inference for mortality is supported by randomisation and an objective endpoint, but constrained by 23% post-randomisation exclusions and an open-label design.

domains.notes: Predominantly blunt trauma cohort (98–99%) with high injury severity (median ISS ~20, high prevalence of polytrauma and TBI) in mature European level-1 trauma systems. Excluded isolated penetrating trauma.

Highly applicable to well-resourced level-1 trauma centers with immediate CT access adjacent to resuscitation bays; limited generalisability to low-resource settings, non-level-1 centers, or penetrating trauma populations.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate: findings apply directly to high-resource blunt trauma systems but cannot be generalized to penetrating trauma or settings with constrained CT availability.

strengths: Pragmatic multicentre RCT conducted in real-world level-1 trauma resuscitation settings.
Objective, clinically relevant primary endpoint (in-hospital mortality).
Standardized, two-step total-body CT imaging protocol.
Comprehensive evaluation of process times, radiation exposure, 6-month readmission, and health economics.
limitations: Open-label design permitting potential performance bias in process metrics.
Substantial post-randomisation exclusions (23% of randomised cohort) creating a modified ITT population.
Modest absolute time savings (8–9 minutes) that may be insufficient to impact survival.
Exclusion of isolated penetrating trauma and extremely unstable patients requiring immediate surgical intervention.

critical_appraisal.summary: A high-quality, pragmatic trial demonstrating that routine immediate total-body CT accelerates diagnostic workflow in blunt major trauma by several minutes but does not alter survival compared to selective CT, while increasing radiation exposure.
strengths: Rigorous multicentre pragmatic design in mature trauma systems
Clear objective primary endpoint coupled with process and health economic data
Standardized CT imaging protocol across all participating centers
weaknesses: Underpowered for subgroup mortality differences (polytrauma, TBI)
Open-label design for time-to-diagnosis process metrics

sections.authors_conclusion: Immediate total-body CT during initial trauma resuscitation does not reduce in-hospital mortality compared with standard conventional imaging and selective CT in patients with severe trauma.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Routine 'pan-scan for all' should not be the universal default; imaging should remain selective and guided by clinical evaluation, vital signs, and mechanism of injury.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult patients with suspected major blunt trauma presenting to high-resource emergency trauma centers.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Total-body CT should be avoided; it means CT should be applied selectively based on clinical indication rather than mandated universally.
implementation_caveats: Time gains from CT are modest (8–9 min) and do not substitute for rapid definitive operative or interventional hemorrhage control.
Radiation exposure is higher with upfront whole-body scanning.
Unstable patients requiring immediate operative resuscitation should not be delayed for pan-scanning.

controversies.notes: Debate over whether a median 8-minute diagnostic time saving is clinically meaningful unless it directly accelerates emergency surgery or angioembolization.
Exclusion of 320 randomised patients (23%) due to consent and eligibility issues raised concerns regarding potential selection bias in the modified ITT cohort.

controversies.topic: RCT neutrality vs observational registry benefits
controversies.notes: REACT-2 refuted earlier observational registry studies showing survival benefits for pan-scanning, demonstrating that registry findings were likely confounded by center volume and quality of care.
The statistically significant increase in 6-month readmissions in the iTBCT group (17% vs 11%, P=0.01) remains mechanistically unexplained.

unresolved_questions: Which specific clinical criteria or predictive rules best identify trauma subgroup populations that experience a true survival benefit from immediate whole-body CT?
What is the mechanism behind the increased 6-month readmission rate observed in the immediate total-body CT group?
Does immediate total-body CT offer survival or functional benefits in high-volume penetrating trauma cohorts?

numbers_to_remember: N=1,083 analysed (541 iTBCT vs 542 selective CT)
Time to diagnosis: 50 min vs 58 min (P<0.0001)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Routine immediate whole-body CT speeds up trauma diagnosis by 8 minutes but does not reduce mortality, supporting selective CT over universal pan-scanning.
